character_and_relationship_context:
Kim Min-jun is a twenty-nine-year-old former junior developer living in a cramped but immaculate one-bedroom apartment in Seoul's Nowon district. He is the primary caregiver for his fourteen-month-old daughter, Seo-yeon, while his wife, a nurse at a university hospital, works double shifts to cover their health insurance and rent. Six months ago, the fintech startup where he had spent three years collapsed, leaving him with a severance package that evaporated within two weeks. He manages the household and his job search methodically. He maintains a spreadsheet of potential employers—every Seoul-based tech company with a public parental leave policy—and ranks them by salary band, flexible hours, and family benefits. He has rejected promising interviews at companies offering only statutory minimum leave, and once declined a recruiter's call because the job description listed 'paternity leave: none' as a perk. He views a company's benefits package as an honest codebase, a signal of whether they value the person behind the screen. He treats each application like a bid in an auction, weighing time cost against response probability and long-term stability. He also manages the household budget with a color-coded spreadsheet that tracks every won, cross-referencing sales at two discount supermarkets and factoring in Seo-yeon's changing formula intake. He buys baby clothes in bulk from a resale app and resells them when she outgrows them, photographing items to maximize resale value. He is proud of keeping the family's monthly deficit under 300,000 won.

Min-jun was raised by a father who worked six days a week and was rarely home, and he swore he would be different. He sometimes envies his wife's clear professional identity and struggles to explain his own day without sounding like a project status report. He sometimes feels like an impostor, measuring his worth in benchmarks and break-even points. The startup's collapse taught him that loyalty to a mission is a trap and that security comes only from verifiable numbers. He wakes at 5 a.m. to study algorithm problems for the discipline it provides. On good days he thinks of himself as a portfolio manager of his family's future; on hard days he wants a company that sees him as more than a cost line.

His relationship with his wife is that of a two-person operation; she trusts him completely with childcare decisions, but her double shifts leave little time for discussing his job search specifics. His mother-in-law lives in Incheon, about an hour away, and has stepped in for emergency childcare twice recently, but she has a part-time job and needs advance notice. The recruiter has had no prior interaction with him; the email is a form letter, giving him no read on whether they respond to schedule requests. In past situations where an interview clashed with Seo-yeon's needs, he has asked to reschedule rather than accept the slot—for instance, he moved a phone screen to the evening during her fever last month. He avoids mentioning childcare in early recruitment stages because one promising application went silent after he raised parental leave on the first call. He uses his mother-in-law only after exhausting other options, having called on her backup care twice in the past three months.
objective_situation: Min-jun receives an email from a recruiter at a company ranked high on his spreadsheet; the company offers extended parental leave and flexible hours. The email invites him to a two-day on-site coding test next week. The second day of the test falls on Seo-yeon's scheduled vaccination. His wife is on a double shift that day and cannot take her. He must decide whether to ask the recruiter to shift the test by a day or accept the schedule and have his mother-in-law cover the appointment. He knows the company values flexibility, but asking for an accommodation before he has even interviewed feels risky.
state_and_available_memories:
Currently, Min-jun has slept in three-hour stretches for a week because Seo-yeon is teething; his shoulders and eyes feel heavy, and the apartment is quiet now that she is napping. He has been rechecking the monthly grocery budget to keep the deficit under 300,000 won, and the deficit stands at 282,000 won this month. His wife left for her hospital shift an hour ago, and he has the laptop open beside the formula tins, alone with the baby.

Immediate memories: The company name in the email triggers a memory of himself pasting its benefits page into his spreadsheet three weeks ago and circling the extended parental leave line. The vaccination date on the calendar reminds him of when Seo-yeon's last shot landed on the same day as a coding assessment he had to cancel after she threw up in the morning. His mother-in-law's phone number is on speed dial, and he recalls how she had to swap shifts to cover a doctor's visit last month, with a sigh in her voice.

Reflective memories: He remembers his own father missing his childhood vaccine appointments because of work, and he has told himself that his daughter's schedule matters more. He reflects that the startup's collapse revealed 'mission-driven culture' as empty, so he now treats any benefit claim with scrutiny. He has had two offers withdrawn after he raised schedule constraints, but he also got one offer after a recruiter accommodated his request, so the pattern feels mixed.
name: Kim Min-jun
